title: 1 Kings 4:1–6
context: Having shown Solomon’s God-given wisdom in judgment, the narrator turns to the structure of his government. A short list names Solomon’s chief officials: priests, scribes, a recorder, the commander of the army, the officer over the district governors, a royal adviser called “the king’s friend,” the steward of the household, and the official over forced labor. Several names carry over from David’s court (compare 2 Samuel 8:15–18; 20:23–26), while others are new. The precise duties attached to some titles are not fully certain, and the mention of Abiathar alongside Zadok sits in some tension with his removal in 1 Kings 2:26–27, which interpreters explain in different ways. Both traditions read the list as evidence of an ordered kingdom in which God’s blessing is worked out through faithful administration.

verses.text: King Solomon was king over all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the simple statement that Solomon was king over all Israel summarizes the stability achieved after the struggles of David’s final years and the succession crisis. The unity of the kingdom is presented as a gift of God that also depended on wise leadership and the loyalty of many people throughout the realm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this verse the fulfillment of God’s promise to establish David’s son on the throne (2 Samuel 7:12). Both traditions agree that the verse marks a high point of national unity, and both recognize that the books of Kings will later show how quickly that unity could be lost when kings turned away from the LORD.

verses.text: These were the princes whom he had: Azariah the son of Zadok, the priest;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the list begins with Azariah the son of Zadok, the priest, placing the priesthood at the head of Solomon’s officials. This ordering suggests that worship and covenant faithfulness were meant to stand at the center of national life, with the king’s officials serving under God’s authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see significance in the priest appearing first, reflecting the close relationship between worship and government in Israel. Both traditions agree that the verse shows a priestly line connected to Zadok continuing in Solomon’s court, consistent with the earlier account of Zadok’s faithfulness during the succession (1 Kings 1:32–40).

verses.text: Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that scribes and a recorder are named, showing that Solomon’s kingdom required written records, correspondence, and administration. Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud also served in David’s court (2 Samuel 8:16), and his continued service suggests continuity and experience carried into the new reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these offices reflect an ordered government in which God’s blessing is expressed through careful administration. Both traditions agree that the verse shows the value of competent, faithful service in ordinary roles, and that the narrator treats the work of scribes and recorders as part of the stable kingdom God had granted.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Benaiah, who carried out Solomon’s judgments in chapter 2, now commands the army, and that Zadok and Abiathar are listed as priests. The mention of Abiathar is surprising after his banishment (1 Kings 2:26–27), and interpreters suggest it may reflect his former status or an earlier stage of the list, though the text does not explain it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the continuity of Benaiah’s loyalty and his reward with high command, and they acknowledge the difficulty raised by Abiathar’s name. Both traditions agree that the list should be read honestly with its tension rather than smoothed over, and that the main point is the establishment of Solomon’s government with trusted officials.

verses.text: Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was chief minister, the king’s friend;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that two sons of Nathan hold important positions: Azariah over the district officers and Zabud as chief minister and the king’s friend. Many interpreters connect them with Nathan the prophet, who supported Solomon’s accession, though the text does not state this, and the title “king’s friend” suggests a trusted adviser.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the verse as highlighting trusted advisers in Solomon’s court, and they note that the possible link to Nathan the prophet is plausible but not certain. Both traditions agree that the verse shows the importance of faithful counsel to a king, and that the office over the officers prepares for the list of district governors that follows.

verses.text: Ahishar was over the household; and Adoniram the son of Abda was over the men subject to forced labor.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ahishar was over the household and Adoniram was over the forced labor. The mention of forced labor is significant, since this burden would later contribute to the division of the kingdom (1 Kings 12:4, 18), showing how policies that seemed practical could carry long-term consequences for the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the reference to forced labor as foreshadowing the tensions that would lead to the kingdom’s division. Both traditions agree that the narrator includes this office without immediate comment, allowing later events to reveal the cost of royal demands, and that even a blessed kingdom faced the danger of oppressive practices.
